title: Find secret keys hiding in your cloud-synced folders
summary: A developer asked Claude Code for a read-only security check of their Mac; it found 49 settings files holding 100 keys and tokens syncing to iCloud.
agent_role: Claude Code searched the Mac in read-only mode and flagged secret files inside synced folders without printing their values. The human then moved the secrets, replaced the exposed keys and turned on stronger iCloud encryption.
outcome: Author reports Claude Code found 49 settings files across 48 projects, 100 plain-text keys and tokens, 10 Telegram bot tokens and 5 Telegram login sessions in iCloud Drive.
what_they_did: The poster keeps their projects folder in iCloud Drive to switch between two Macs. They asked Claude Code for a read-only security check: find secrets in synced folders and never print the values. Claude Code flagged that the hidden settings files holding passwords and keys were syncing along with the projects.
how_it_went: The author says it found 49 such files across 48 projects, with 100 keys and tokens in plain text, including 10 Telegram bot tokens. They moved the secrets out, replaced the exposed keys and turned on Apple's Advanced Data Protection.
worth_knowing: Moving secrets out of the synced folder is not enough. Any key that already synced should be treated as exposed and replaced.
prompt: Run a read-only security check on this computer. Do not change, move or delete anything. Look through my synced folders ([iCloud Drive / Dropbox / OneDrive]) and my projects folder at [path] for files that hold secrets, such as .env files, API keys, tokens and saved login sessions. Never print the secret values themselves. Give me a list of each file, what kind of secret it seems to hold, and whether it is in a synced folder. Then suggest a plan to move the secrets somewhere safer and which keys I should replace. Wait for my approval before making any changes.

curation.rationale: A concrete, read-only security check by Claude Code that found real, specific problems: secret keys sitting in cloud-synced folders. The exact prompt is shared and the fix steps are clear, so most readers can repeat it.
